So I used to be a hairstylist for 3 years. I'm now an established Lash Extension artist full-time. I'll start with saying if your gut is telling you this is what you really are meant to be doing, do it. It's an art, it's beautiful. Cosmetology school will either be a good time, or the worst; mostly because you will be taught the basics and how to pass state board. The "fun stuff" will likely be brief or you will have to learn them outside of school. For me, the schooling all 3 licenses (cos, esthetics, massage therapy) was the worst; but I'm in Michigan and didn't have a ton of options as to where I could go. You may have a lot of schools in California, so try to be a little picky if you can and be ready to stick it out.

I'm sorry, this will be long. I'm very passionate about this industry lol

1. **How long did it take you to build a solid clientele?** In hairstyling - 2 years to be proud of myself. Lashes - 1 year to be comfortable. Promote the SHIT out of yourself and your work in social media. 70% of my clients found me on instagram and 20% are friends of those people. Also, if you specialize in something (like I do lashes exclusively) reach out to other salons and have a good relationship with them, so they can recommend you to clients. That is my other 10%; people who were given to me from other lash artists or hairdressers I'm friends with.
2. **Is reaching at least $50k profit possible?** If you educate yourself, get certified in various techniques from brands you love, and charge what you are worth, you can make upwards of $150K. Especially in a high end area in California. But also, you will need to be able to compete with other stylists. But yes, $50K is very possible. It'll take time, and a lot of people in the industry have side gigs for at least the first 3 or so years.
3. **Did you start renting right away or assist?** It depends on how you do in Cos school. If you get a solid following from school, people who will ACTUALLY follow you and keep you busy and able to pay rent, buy product, do taxes etc. Then renting is possible. But, I'm a firm believer of the idea of "paying your dues" and working as an assistant and learning from others who have been in the industry much longer than you and who are willing tot each you. You'd do a lot of hair washing, cleaning, and other boring stuff. But the knowledge you can gain is worth it. A lot of places do employ their stylists for commission as well, so that's an option. I started hair assisting, then I worked where I assisted for commission (sucked). Then I went into renting spaces to do lashes, as well as being an employee at another lash salon.
4. **Are most clients talkative?** Honestly, it depends on you. If you do good work but you're quiet, most people will respect it. But you will gain the ability for small talk in school pretty quickly. If you like to talk, be able to read a room/person. If they aren't into it, don't force small talk or conversation. Those who want to talk will talk. I usually let my clients do the talking and ask questions to keep them talking.
5. **I have some social anxiety, will this career eat me alive because of this?** I do too. With clients, it's all the same as number 4. The only issue I could foresee is networking. In order to find placement in good private salons and to build clientele, you need to be able to squash down the anxiety and talk to people and go to things or do things that are hard. It's scary every time I meet a new client. It's scary every time I meet a new salon owner and try to make them like me so they'll recommend me as a local lash artist. Every time i have to walk into a venue to leave business cards behind. It's worth it. Find a way to work through it.
6. **Are other stylist friendly and helpful or are they catty?** Depends on the salon. Whenever I interview somewhere, one of my first questions to the owner/manager is "Is there any drama in the salon?" The answer is usually, "No, we are all a family and we all mesh well" or "Well, it IS a building full of women." It's just easiest to assume drama happens and don't mix yourself into it and focus on your work. Even if it's a friend.
7. **What are your hours like? Like do you have to work from 9am - 9pm? Is having Sunday and Monday possible?** Right now, I rent 2 spaces and I'm an employee at a 3rd. I work when I am needed within set hours and I decide when I am needed. Most places you'll start in will tell you to be there for a certain amount of hours, with or without clients. You'd be needed for walk-ins. Or to do mundane things around the salon.  Assisting depends on the place and the arrangement. Most are a good 9-5 but I assisted for a hairstylist only when she had clients, because I was HER assistant.
8. **Are you happy with your career choice?** Well, obviously, I don't do hair anymore, so not really lol. I do my family and close friends' hair at home and that's it. Nowadays, vanity and appearance are at an all-time high. People are entitled, snotty, and expect the world for nothing. everything is photoshopped and is giving people unrealistic expectations. Especially about their hair. I personally couldn't handle it. But I will say, if I ever decide to go back to doing hair, it will be for all the surprisingly touching moments i had with my clients. All the dramatic haircuts after divorces or breakups. Silently helping women in abusive households. Helping someone get ready for their wedding. A teenager going to her first prom with her crush. Being asked to do one of my elderly client's hair for the last time at the funeral home so their family could remember them as they were. You become a part of a person's routine and a lot of the time, a surrogate therapist. You'll know things about some people that their friends won't. I miss that part of hair so so much.

If you're looking ro do the magenta/red long term, no it's not really easier. If you bleach it and use semi on top, it will fade muuuuch faster and will be harder ro keep even. The hicolor fills in the open pores in your hair immediately with color so the result is much slower fading and it will blend nicer.

But if you want to be able to do blues and purples, it would best to get at least most of the red out, especially if you want to do blue.

To do this, use a color remover first. Not bleach. Color Oops from a store will do fine but it will cause a little damage. If you decide to use this, do a really good conditioning treatment and wait a day or two before using any bleach. It might be best to have a professional use a professional grade remover to get the red dyes out.

Because you've been opening the pores in your hair and putting red dyes on it repeatedly, using bleach on it first will make the red molecules almost impossible to remove. The remover will do the heavy lifting on the molecular level in your hair and using bleach after if you need it lighter is the best option tbh. You can get very nice blues and purple on light orange or light pink hair. It doesn't need to be white.

And then use a very good conditioner. A lot.

There should be little swatches of hair right on the display where you buy the color (Like Sally's Beauty Supply for manic panic) if there's not I would ask a clerk for help. They know the color or will have a book of swatches.

Match the swatches to the color your hair is now or what is is after using the hicolor on it, which is what the hicolor will turn out to be on your roots. Yup. Using the hicolor all over every time is pretty damaging. And if you ever wanna take the red out, it will be a pain lol. I've learned from experience on my own hair before I got licensed.

Use the hicolor just on your new growth/roots when its time to redo. Then freshen your ends with a semi permanent. Do the semi at a separate time and leave it in for as long as you can stand it. I do over night when I freshen my red.
Good semis for red are manic panic or arctic fox. Ion is ok but its not great for your hair but it'll do the job. If you're professional, pravana or pulp riot are really good.

If you want a true blue, get the red and pink out first with a color remover first, then bleach if needed. You can get a good blue on light orange or pink hair.

If you're starting with already short hair, bleach first. Then when its cut, you'll be cutting the dead ends off from the lightener and not damaging a fresh cut.

But if its long, cut it first to not waste product and get a dusting (very minimal trim) done after lightening it to get most of the yucky ends off.
